open_questions/0.rationale:
This is a HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH rather than a KNOWLEDGE_GAP because the evidence is not absent - four independent NDRG1-deficient models exist, three rodent and one canine, and all have had their myelin phenotype characterised in detail. What is uncertain is their translational validity for the arm of the disease that matters clinically, which is precisely the arm that has not been characterised to the same standard. The stretcher mouse and the hypomorphic Ndrg1 knockout were compared head to head and neither displays the early severe axonal loss typical of the human disease, with regenerative capacity explicitly unimpaired; the independent CRISPR Ndrg1-/- mouse likewise shows no apparent axonal loss despite faithful demyelination; and the canine model is described as a mixed polyneuropathy without the deafness that defines the human disorder.
The consequence is precise and constraining, and the rodent and canine models have to be stated separately because they fail differently. No rodent model reconstructs the step from Schwann-cell NDRG1 loss to axonal degeneration: all three reproduce demyelination and none the early severe axonal loss. The Greyhound is not in that position - it has prominent axonal pathology, with severe axonal atrophy, dropout of large myelinated fibres, Wallerian degeneration and neurogenic muscle atrophy. What has not been shown for the canine model is the feature that actually defines the human lesion: that the axonal loss is early and disproportionate to the demyelination rather than a late consequence of it. Nobody has assessed it for that, which is a different and weaker statement than failing to reproduce it.
The practical consequence is unchanged. The gene-discovery work framed CMT4D as a disease of impaired axon-glia interaction, and axonal loss is what produces the disability. Any preclinical result in the rodent models - including the observation that a treatment window exists before the four-week onset of myelin thinning - speaks to the demyelinating arm only, and must not be curated or read as addressing the axonal arm. The canine line is the one place the axonal arm might be testable, which is why the proposed long-axon experiment below uses it.

open_questions/1.rationale: Twenty-six years after the gene was found, the molecular function of NDRG1 remains unresolved, and a 2013 clinical report still opens by saying so. What makes this a genuine gap rather than an unfinished literature is that the field has actively excluded candidates: the stretcher work found no support for roles in growth arrest, terminal differentiation, gene expression regulation or proteasomal degradation, leaving vesicular trafficking as the surviving hypothesis largely by elimination. The positive evidence for trafficking is real but indirect - Rab4a compartment enlargement and failed LDL receptor recycling in cell lines, lipid-vesicle binding by the purified protein, and a timing coincidence between demyelination and peak myelin growth in mouse. None of it measures membrane flux in a Schwann cell, and the protein is a hydrolase-fold member with no demonstrated catalytic activity, so the possibility that its relevant function is something not yet tested is not closed.

open_questions/2.rationale: Three independent lines of observation point at the central nervous system: subcortical white matter abnormalities in a non-Roma p.Arg148*-homozygous family, cerebellar, medullary and upper cervical cord atrophy in an Italian patient with a different allele, and prolonged brainstem auditory evoked potential interpeak latencies that appear before hearing complaints. NDRG1 is ubiquitously expressed, so central involvement is biologically unsurprising. But none of these is decisive: evoked-potential delay is equally compatible with conduction failure in the proximal eighth-nerve segment, imaging findings come from single families, and no neuropathological examination of CMT4D central tissue has been reported. The authors who first reported the white matter lesions themselves called for further study rather than claiming a central phenotype. This entry therefore keeps the auditory node separate from the somatic chain rather than asserting a shared mechanism.

open_questions/3.rationale: The reviewed human reports establish these observations, but do not identify a causal route for each. Scoliosis is quantified without a demonstrated paraspinal denervation or other spinal mechanism. The two siblings with dysphagia and vocal cord paralysis have no reported localization sufficient to distinguish cranial neuropathy from central motor involvement; vocal cord paralysis causing respiratory insufficiency is explicitly established and is represented. Cognitive delay lacks a defined developmental or neuropathological substrate. White matter lesions, cerebellar atrophy, medullary atrophy and cervical cord atrophy come from different limited reports whose authors do not establish whether each is a primary central consequence of NDRG1 loss or secondary degeneration. The visual evoked-potential abnormality establishes visual pathway dysfunction, but not its cause or correspondence to those structural findings. Motor delay is directly observed in some molecularly confirmed patients while other cohorts have normal milestones; the reviewed sources do not connect the delayed milestones to a defined early peripheral lesion. These uncertainties concern causal attribution, not a requirement to reconstruct every molecular intermediate. The peripheral glia-to-axon route and the auditory route are represented with their stated uncertainty.

evidence.snippet: The deletion 18p syndrome is one of the most common chromosome abnormalities. The medical problems are mental and postnatal growth retardation, and sometimes malformations of the heart and brain.
evidence.explanation: Establishes 18p deletion as the initiating lesion producing mental and growth retardation and structural malformations.

evidence.snippet: Genotype-phenotype correlation of the seven subjects suggests a correlation between the extent of the deleted region and the mental development.
evidence.explanation: Supports that haploinsufficiency burden (deletion extent) drives the neurocognitive phenotype, the basis for a contiguous-gene mechanism.

steps/3.description: Terminal or interstitial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 18 removes one copy of multiple dosage-sensitive genes, producing a contiguous-gene haploinsufficiency syndrome. The extent of the deleted region and which dosage-sensitive genes are rendered hemizygous determine the phenotypic spectrum, including a critical region for intellectual disability and the distal location of genes (e.g., TGIF1) underlying midline brain defects and growth-hormone deficiency.

evidence.snippet: The phenotype of monosomy 18p varies widely, the main clinical manifestations being mental and growth retardation, and craniofacial dysmorphism. Clinical features also include growth hormone (GH) deficiency, or holoprosencephaly (HPE).
evidence.explanation: Links monosomy 18p to holoprosencephaly and GH deficiency within the midline-defect spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Haploinsufficiency for TGIF, mapped to 18p11.3, is not generally sufficient to cause HPE.
evidence.explanation: Supports TGIF1 hemizygosity as the candidate HPE mechanism while noting its incomplete penetrance, consistent with the modifier-dependent model.

steps/4.description: TGIF1 (at distal 18p11.3) encodes a homeodomain transcriptional regulator in the TGF-beta / NODAL signaling pathway that is critical for dorsal-ventral patterning and midline development during embryogenesis. Haploinsufficiency is an established genomic mechanism for holoprosencephaly (HPE) and HPE microforms, with incomplete penetrance; in 18p deletion carriers other genetic or environmental factors modulate expressivity.

evidence.snippet: There might be a critical region for the mental retardation located between 18p11.1 and 18p11.21.
evidence.explanation: Supports a dosage-dependent critical region underlying the intellectual disability phenotype.

steps/5.description: Hemizygosity of dosage-sensitive 18p genes impairs brain development, producing intellectual disability and global developmental delay. A critical region for intellectual disability lies between 18p11.1 and 18p11.21, and deletion extent correlates with cognitive outcome.

evidence.snippet: Immunoglobulin (Ig) A deficiency has long been recognized in patients with chromosome 18 abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Documents IgA deficiency as a recognized immune manifestation of chromosome 18 abnormalities, including 18p deletion syndrome.

steps/6.description: 18p hemizygosity is associated with immunoglobulin deficiency (most notably IgA, but also IgG and IgM), predisposing to recurrent infection and autoimmunity.

evidence.snippet: These findings suggest that the distal region on 18p is involved in the main clinical features, and GH deficiency, in 18p deletions.
evidence.explanation: Maps the GH-deficiency phenotype to distal 18p hemizygosity.

steps/7.description: Distal 18p hemizygosity is associated with isolated growth-hormone deficiency and, less commonly, hypopituitarism, contributing to postnatal growth retardation and short stature. The distal 18p region is implicated in the GH-deficiency phenotype.

evidence.snippet: The individuals have some typical features, which might be easy to overlook and which are: ptosis, strabismus, hypertelorism, broad flat nose, micrognathia, big and low set ears.
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the characteristic craniofacial dysmorphic features of the syndrome.

steps/8.description: Reduced dosage of 18p developmental genes perturbs craniofacial and periocular morphogenesis, producing a recognizable but subtle facial gestalt with ptosis, strabismus, hypertelorism, broad flat nose, micrognathia, and large low-set ears.

evidence.snippet:
A Case of 18p Chromosomal Deletion Encompassing GNAL in a Patient With 
Dystonia-Parkinsonism.
evidence.explanation: Reports a patient with an 18p deletion encompassing GNAL who presented with dystonia-parkinsonism, supporting GNAL hemizygosity as a movement-disorder mechanism.

steps/9.description: GNAL (at 18p11.21) encodes the alpha subunit of the olfactory G protein (G-alpha-olf), and point mutations in GNAL are a major cause of adult-onset dystonia. Hemizygosity in 18p deletion carriers confers a low-penetrance (~3%) risk of dystonia through impaired striatal G-protein signaling.

evidence.snippet: Digenic inheritance of a SMCHD1 mutation and a moderately sized D4Z4 repeat on a facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) permissive genetic background of chromosome 4 can cause FSHD type 2 (FSHD2).
evidence.explanation: Supports SMCHD1 hemizygosity from 18p deletion as a conditional digenic risk factor for FSHD2.

steps/10.description:
SMCHD1 (at 18p11.32) is a chromatin modifier that maintains heavy methylation of the D4Z4 macrosatellite repeat on chromosome 4q35, repressing the DUX4 retrogene. In 18p deletion carriers, SMCHD1 hemizygosity combined with a permissive (moderately sized) D4Z4 allele on chromosome 4 can cause facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy type 2 (FSHD2) through digenic inheritance, DUX4 derepression, and muscle degeneration.
The digenic claim here belongs to FSHD2, not to 18p deletion syndrome. 18p deletion is a chromosomal, usually de novo event, so this entry binds no digenic inheritance term (HP:0010984) and is not a member of the Digenic and Oligogenic Disorders grouping; Facioscapulohumeral Muscular Dystrophy is a member, on exactly this SMCHD1-plus-permissive-4qA mechanism. What 18p deletion contributes is one route to the SMCHD1 hemizygosity that FSHD2 needs.

evidence.snippet: All the four children with a deletion in the centromeric region at 18p11.1 had a mental retardation (MR).
evidence.explanation: Documents intellectual disability (historical term "mental retardation") in 18p deletion patients.

steps/11.description: Cognitive impairment, typically in the mild to borderline intellectual disability range, is a core feature; deletion extent correlates with cognitive outcome.

evidence.snippet: The mitochondrial elongation factor Tu (EF-Tu), encoded by the TUFM gene, is a GTPase, which is part of the mitochondrial protein translation mechanism.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the gene product and its GTPase role in mitochondrial translation.

evidence.snippet: Yeast and mammalian cell systems proved the pathogenic role of the mutant alleles by functional complementation in vivo.
evidence.explanation: Experimental demonstration that the identified alleles are the cause rather than incidental variants.

steps/1.description: Biallelic missense variants in TUFM reduce the function of mitochondrial elongation factor Tu. EF-Tu is a GTPase whose job is to bind charged aminoacyl-tRNAs and escort them to the mitochondrial ribosome, so a hypomorphic EF-Tu limits the rate at which the ribosome can be supplied with substrate. The pathogenicity of the alleles was established experimentally by functional complementation rather than inferred from conservation alone.

evidence.snippet: If it is activated, it delivers the aminoacyl-tRNAs to the mitochondrial ribosome.
evidence.explanation: States the specific elongation function that is lost, namely delivery of aminoacyl-tRNA to the mitoribosome.

evidence.snippet: Genetic investigation involving patients with defective mitochondrial translation led us to the discovery of novel mutations in the mitochondrial elongation factor G1 (EFG1) in one affected baby and, for the first time, in the mitochondrial elongation factor Tu (EFTu) in another one.
evidence.explanation: Places these patients within the class of defective mitochondrial translation, which is the phenotype the gene search started from.

steps/2.description: Mitochondria run a translation apparatus of their own, separate from the cytosolic one, dedicated to the thirteen proteins encoded by mitochondrial DNA. EF-Tu is a shared component of that apparatus, not a subunit-specific factor, so limiting it throttles synthesis of all thirteen products simultaneously rather than any one of them selectively.

evidence.snippet: leading to combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 4 (COXPD4) characterized by severe early-onset lactic acidosis and progressive fatal infantile encephalopathy
evidence.explanation: Names the combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency that TUFM variants produce.

steps/3.description: Complexes I, III, IV and V each contain at least one mtDNA-encoded subunit and cannot be assembled in normal amounts when mitochondrial translation is limiting. Complex II contains none and is spared. That pattern - several complexes down together with complex II normal - is the diagnostic signature that distinguishes a translation defect from a lesion in an individual complex, and it is what the "combined" in the disease name denotes.

evidence.snippet: leading to combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 4 (COXPD4) characterized by severe early-onset lactic acidosis and progressive fatal infantile encephalopathy
evidence.explanation: Identifies the combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency whose downstream consequence is the cellular energy deficit this node records.

steps/4.description: With four of the five respiratory complexes under-assembled, cells cannot meet their ATP demand by oxidative phosphorylation and fall back on glycolysis. Tissues differ in how much slack they have, which is why the organs that fail are the ones with the highest and least flexible oxidative demand.

evidence.snippet: Both patients were affected by severe lactic acidosis and rapidly progressive, fatal encephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: Reports the severe lactic acidosis in the index patients.

steps/5.description: Lactate produced by glycolytic compensation accumulates in blood and cerebrospinal fluid, producing the severe, early-onset and persistent lactic acidosis that is the most consistent laboratory finding in this disease and the one feature present across every reported phenotypic variant.

evidence.snippet: the EFTu-mutant patient had severe infantile macrocystic leukodystrophy with micropolygyria
evidence.explanation: Describes the neuroimaging and neuropathological phenotype of the index TUFM patient.

evidence.snippet: The condition is characterized by microcephaly, severe early-onset lactic acidosis, and progressive, often fatal, infantile encephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: Characterises the core clinical triad of the disease.

steps/6.description: The dominant clinical picture in the classical presentation: rapidly progressive, frequently fatal encephalopathy from the neonatal or early infantile period, with microcephaly. Neuroimaging in the index EF-Tu patient showed severe infantile macrocystic leukodystrophy with micropolygyria, and MONDO's description of the disease likewise records polymicrogyria with white-matter abnormality - a malformation of cortical development alongside the destructive white-matter change, indicating that the energy deficit acts during brain formation and not only after it.

evidence.snippet: The patient presented here expands the phenotypic features of TUFM-related disease, exhibiting lactic acidosis and dilated cardiomyopathy without progressive encephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: Reports the cardiomyopathy-predominant presentation that this node records.

steps/7.description: Cardiac involvement has been the presenting and dominant problem in two patients, and it took a different form in each: a dilated cardiomyopathy in an infant with lactic acidosis but no progressive encephalopathy, and a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in the only reported adult. TUFM therefore belongs in the differential for metabolic cardiomyopathy of either morphology, and these two cases are the clearest evidence that the disease is not obligately neurological. Nothing explains why the morphology differs.

evidence.snippet: He presents with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and chronic kidney failure, which have not previously been reported in this condition.
evidence.explanation: Reports hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in a genetically confirmed adult patient.

steps/8.description: Reported in an adult proband, alongside chronic kidney failure, as a presentation not previously described in this condition. Note this is a different cardiac phenotype from the dilated cardiomyopathy of the infantile-onset patient, so TUFM is associated with both.

evidence.explanation: Reports micropolygyria, the older spelling of polymicrogyria, in the index TUFM patient.

evidence.snippet: the EFTu-mutant patient had severe infantile macrocystic leukodystrophy with micropolygyria
evidence.explanation: Reports the macrocystic leukodystrophy in the index TUFM patient.

edges/1.description: Reduced EF-Tu activity limits delivery of charged aminoacyl-tRNAs to the mitochondrial ribosome, which is the elongation step itself.

edges/2.description: The thirteen mtDNA-encoded subunits are distributed across complexes I, III, IV and V, so under-supplying all of them makes those four complexes fail together while complex II, built entirely from nuclear-encoded subunits, is spared.

edges/4.description: Glycolytic compensation converts the accumulating pyruvate to lactate, which leaves the cell.

edges/5.description: The developing brain has a high and inflexible oxidative demand, which is why it is the organ most consistently and most severely affected.

edges/6.description: Cardiac muscle is likewise oxidative-dependent. The step itself is as direct as the encephalopathy branch; what is unexplained is why it dominates in some patients and is absent in others, which is recorded as an open question rather than as missing intermediate steps.

edges/7.description: The clinical and laboratory manifestation of the accumulated lactate.

edges/8.description: The clinical manifestation by which this node is recognised.

edges/10.description: A malformation of cortical development, so this edge asserts the energy deficit acts during brain formation rather than only degrading a formed brain.

edges/11.description: The destructive white-matter component, reported as macrocystic leukodystrophy in the index patient.

edges/13.description: The alternative cardiac morphology, reported in the adult patient.

evidence.snippet: novel mutations in the mitochondrial elongation factor G1 (EFG1) in one affected baby and, for the first time, in the mitochondrial elongation factor Tu (EFTu) in another one
evidence.explanation: The founding report identifying TUFM/EF-Tu as a human disease gene.

open_questions/0.rationale:
Half of this claim is now measured and half is not, and the two should not be read as equally supported. Reduced complex I, III and IV activity is directly reported on endomyocardial biopsy in an adult proband. Preserved complex II is not: no source cited here reports a complex II value in a TUFM patient, and the sparing is inferred from the fact that complex II contains no mtDNA-encoded subunit. That inference is sound biochemistry and is why the disease class is called combined, but it remains an inference.
It matters because the discriminating value of the test is asserted to come from complex II being normal. A curator who finds a series reporting complex II activity in TUFM patients should replace the inference with the measured values and close this gap.

open_questions/1.rationale: All reported alleles are missense and all patients share severe lactic acidosis, so the divergence is not a simple null-versus-hypomorph difference in the way it often is for other recessive disorders. The recurrent p.Arg339Gln allele has been reported in several patients, which should make allele-matched comparison possible, but no study has related residual EF-Tu activity to which organ fails. Until that is done, the branch from energy failure to cardiomyopathy is drawn as indirect and variably expressed, and the entry cannot say what determines the split.

open_questions/2.rationale:
TUFM is reported to interact with the autophagy machinery and with NLRX1, and several viruses exploit it to dampen type I interferon responses. If those functions are also lost in patients, the disease could have an immunological or autophagic component that the pure-translation model does not predict.
No reported COXPD4 patient has been described with an infection phenotype or an autophagy defect, and no study has tested whether the patient missense alleles affect these interactions as opposed to the translation function. The entry therefore models COXPD4 strictly as a translation defect. This is recorded so a curator does not later mistake the absence of an immunological arm for an oversight; the literature simply has not asked the question in this disease.

evidence.snippet: The predominant cause of complete C2 deficiency is a 28‐bp deletion (rs9332736) in the exon/intron boundary of exon 6.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the causal variant and its molecular consequence.

evidence.snippet: Pulse-chase biosynthetic labeling experiments indicated that the C111Y mutant C2 was retained by transfected COS cells and secreted only in minimal amounts.
evidence.explanation: Transfection and pulse-chase labelling show the type II mechanism is retention and failed secretion, not absent transcript.

steps/1.description: The predominant type I allele carries a 28-bp deletion at the exon 6 exon/intron boundary, introducing an early stop codon so that no C2 protein reaches plasma. Type II alleles instead permit synthesis but block secretion.

evidence.snippet: Reduced C2 levels in plasma (P = 2 × 10-9 ) and impaired function of the classical complement pathway (P = 0.03) were detected in SLE patients with heterozygous C2 deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that reduced C2 translates into measurably impaired classical pathway function in patients.

steps/2.description: C2 is an obligate component of the classical pathway C3 convertase C4b2a. Its absence blocks classical-pathway C3 cleavage, measurable as absent CH50. The lectin pathway converges on the same C4b2a convertase — MASP-2 cleaves C4 and C2 — so its effector arm fails too; only the alternative pathway (C3bBb) remains intact, which is why lysis is preserved and the phenotype is milder than a C3 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: About 25% of C2-deficient homozygotes have increased susceptibility to severe bacterial infections.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the infection-susceptible fraction of C2-deficient homozygotes.

evidence.snippet: Our study confirms the strong association of meningococcal infections with terminal pathway deficiency and highlights the risk of pneumococcal and auto-immune diseases in the classical and alternative pathways.
evidence.explanation: Contrasts the pneumococcal and autoimmune risk of classical-pathway deficiency with the meningococcal risk of terminal-pathway deficiency.

steps/3.description: Without classical-pathway C3b deposition on encapsulated organisms, chiefly Streptococcus pneumoniae, phagocytes cannot engage them efficiently through complement receptors.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, complete C2 deficiency is one of the most common complement deficiencies, with an estimated prevalence of 1:20,000 in the Swedish population and a penetrance for SLE of ~25%
evidence.explanation: Establishes complete C2 deficiency as a monogenic SLE risk factor with roughly 25% penetrance.

steps/4.description: Classical-pathway activity is required to solubilise immune complexes and to opsonise apoptotic cells for silent clearance. Without it, both persist.

evidence.snippet: in C2 deﬁcient patients included AID ( n = 11, 24.4%)
evidence.explanation: 11 of the 45 C2-deficient patients with clinical data had autoimmune disease. Graded PARTIAL: "AID" in this paper means autoimmune disease broadly, not SLE — the same paper reports SLE separately (16/51, 31.4%) for a different cohort slice. So this supports loss of tolerance as an outcome of C2 deficiency without quantifying lupus specifically, and it is not a replication of the 25% SLE penetrance figure.

steps/5.description: Sustained exposure to uncleared nuclear autoantigen drives loss of B- and T-cell tolerance and anti-nuclear autoantibody production. This is the accepted explanation for the SLE association, but the step from impaired clearance to autoantibody production has not been demonstrated directly in C2-deficient patients — see the knowledge gap below.

evidence.snippet: About 25% of C2-deficient homozygotes have increased susceptibility to severe bacterial infections.
evidence.explanation: Directly reports the proportion with increased bacterial susceptibility among homozygotes.

evidence.snippet: Half of C2D patients (26/45, 57.8%) presented with recurrent or severe infections mostly due to S. pneumoniae (n = 14, 53.8%).
evidence.explanation: A later and larger cohort of diagnosed C2D patients reports a much higher infection rate and names Streptococcus pneumoniae as the predominant organism. Curated alongside the 25% figure rather than replacing it.

steps/6.description: Recurrent invasive pyogenic infection, predominantly pneumococcal. Reported frequency spans a wide range — about 25% of C2-deficient homozygotes in the Sjoholm/Johnson series, against 57.8% of diagnosed C2D patients in the later French cohort. The two are not in conflict so much as differently ascertained; see notes.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, complete C2 deficiency is one of the most common complement deficiencies, with an estimated prevalence of 1:20,000 in the Swedish population and a penetrance for SLE of ~25%
evidence.explanation: States the SLE penetrance of complete C2 deficiency.

steps/7.description: SLE develops in roughly 25% of individuals with complete C2 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Rheumatological disease, mainly systemic lupus erythematosus was present in 43% of the patients.
evidence.explanation: Gives the 43% figure and states that SLE is the main but not the sole component, which is why this record is broader than the SLE phenotype and does not replace it.

steps/8.description:
Rheumatological disease of any kind, reported in 43% of a 40-patient Swedish C2-deficient cohort. Curated alongside the separately recorded Systemic Lupus Erythematosus rather than instead of it, because the source names SLE as the dominant component but not the whole of it — the two records should not be added together.
What the non-SLE remainder consists of is not curated, and the reason is worth recording. A deep-research report for this disease names Henoch-Schonlein purpura, polymyositis, arthralgia and glomerulonephritis, attributing them to Orphanet. That attribution could not be verified: the cited cohort abstract does not name them, and ORPHA:169147 is not in this repository's reference cache and cannot be built here because the Orphadata bulk XML is not present. The list is therefore left out rather than curated on a report's word.

edges/1.description: Without C2 there is no C4b2a, so the classical pathway cannot generate C3 convertase activity.

edges/2.description: Failure to deposit C3b on encapsulated organisms impairs opsonophagocytic clearance.

edges/3.description: Classical pathway activity is required to solubilise immune complexes and clear apoptotic cells; its loss permits their persistence.

edges/4.description: Failure of opsonophagocytic clearance manifests as recurrent invasive pyogenic infection.

edges/5.description: Persisting apoptotic debris is a sustained source of nuclear autoantigen.

evidence.snippet: Rheumatological disease, mainly systemic lupus erythematosus was present in 43% of the patients.
evidence.explanation: The cohort figure this edge carries, and the source of the contrast with the narrower SLE edge drawn from the same node.

edges/6.description: The same loss of tolerance produces rheumatological disease more broadly than SLE alone — 43% of the Swedish cohort against the ~25% SLE penetrance curated elsewhere in this entry. The two edges are drawn separately because the figures are not the same patients counted twice: SLE is the dominant component of the broader category, not the whole of it.

edges/7.description: Loss of tolerance manifests as clinical systemic lupus erythematosus in roughly a quarter of individuals with complete C2 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: The predominant cause of complete C2 deficiency is a 28‐bp deletion (rs9332736) in the exon/intron boundary of exon 6.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the predominant causal allele.

evidence.snippet: Type 1 C2 deficiency is the most common complement alteration, due in 95% of cases to a homozygous 28-bp deletion in the C2 gene
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the type I share at 95%, putting a number on the "predominates" claim in this record's notes.

evidence.snippet: A less common type 2 C2 deficiency that represents 5–7% of the cases
evidence.explanation: The complementary figure for type II alleles, which the notes describe qualitatively as acting by blocking secretion.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic C2 loss-of-function causes complete deficiency. The type I 28-bp deletion predominates; type II alleles act by blocking secretion.

evidence.snippet: Heterozygous C2 deficiency-when present in combination with a low C4A copy number-substantially increased the risk of SLE (odds ratio [OR] 10.2 [95% confidence interval (95% CI) 3.5-37.0])
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the interaction between heterozygous C2 deficiency and low C4A copy number.

genes/1.notes: Low C4A copy number combined with heterozygous C2 deficiency substantially raises SLE and primary Sjogren risk and lowers age at diagnosis, so C4A dose modifies the phenotype of partial C2 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Post-vaccination IgG antibodies against pneumococci serotype 6B and 23F at a concentration ≥1.0mg/L was found in similar frequency in C2D persons and controls.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the antibody response itself is intact in C2 deficiency, which is what makes vaccination worth giving.

evidence.snippet: In conclusion, the C2D persons benefited from the vaccination and achieve an increased phagocytic capacity.
evidence.explanation: The authors' summary judgement on benefit, resting on the opsonophagocytic assay rather than on a clinical infection endpoint.

evidence.snippet: should receive prophylactic penicillin therapy and be considered for both pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccinations
evidence.explanation: States the standard recommendation. The sentence it comes from names the target organisms as Streptococcus pneumoniae, and less frequently Neisseria meningitides and Haemophilus influenzae type B; the quote is cut before that clause because the source interleaves its own bracketed reference markers there, which the snippet validator strips.

treatments/0.description: Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccination is the primary preventive intervention, and it works in C2 deficiency for a mechanistically specific reason. C2-deficient individuals mount normal antibody titres — the block is in effector function, not in the humoral response — and those antibodies restore opsonophagocytosis by driving complement activation through the alternative pathway, bypassing the missing C2 step. Vaccination therefore does not repair the classical pathway; it routes around it.

evidence.snippet: Post-vaccination sera from C2D persons showed poor complement-mediated opsonization and phagocytosis of pneumococci by granulocytes when depending on classical and lectin pathway activation only, but increased (p=0.007) and equaled that of the normal controls when also alternative pathway activation was allowed due to antibody-dependent C2 bypass activation.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the bypass as the mechanism by which vaccination corrects the opsonophagocytic defect, and shows directly that the correction requires alternative-pathway activation rather than repair of the classical arm.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Vaccine-induced antibody permits antibody-dependent alternative-pathway activation, which restores granulocyte phagocytosis of pneumococci to control levels despite the classical-pathway block.

evidence.snippet: Antibiotic prophylaxis was also started, initially with intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin every 21 d, replaced by oral phenoxymethylpenicillin in 2002 and currently with oral amoxicillin in a single daily dose.
evidence.explanation: Documents the agents and the switch across two decades of follow-up, which is where the two bound therapeutic agents come from.

evidence.snippet: Our data show that early diagnosis, use of vaccinations and antibiotic prophylaxis may allow a normal life in hereditary C2 deficiency, which can be characterized using functional and genetic methods.
evidence.explanation: The favourable claim, and the reason it is graded INDIRECT: the outcome is two brothers observed without a comparator, so the absence of infection supports the strategy only by inference from an uncontrolled series.

evidence.snippet: Age of the patient and use of prophylactic antibiotics were not associated with subsequent infection risk.
evidence.explanation: The largest cohort addressing the question finds no protective association for prophylactic antibiotics. Recorded as REFUTE against the efficacy claim rather than omitted, because a treatment block that cited only the two-patient favourable series would misrepresent the evidence base.

treatments/1.description: Long-term prophylactic penicillin is recommended alongside vaccination. The evidence for it is weaker than the recommendation's ubiquity suggests, and the entry records both sides rather than the favourable one: a 21-year two-brother follow-up reports no severe or invasive infection under combined vaccination and prophylaxis, while the 77-patient European registry found no association between prophylactic antibiotic use and subsequent infection risk. The registry also found prescribing varied by country rather than by patient, which is what a practice without a settled evidence base looks like.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Prophylaxis acts on the clinical endpoint rather than on the complement lesion: it suppresses the encapsulated-organism infections that the opsonisation defect permits, without restoring classical-pathway function. That is why it is drawn to the phenotype and not to a mechanism node — and why the evidence for it is contested, since an intervention acting downstream of an unrepaired defect is the kind whose benefit is hardest to demonstrate.

open_questions/0.rationale: Penetrance for SLE is roughly 25% for C2 against around 90% for C1q, even though both abolish classical-pathway function. The gradient implies that the C1 complex contributes to tolerance beyond convertase formation, or that modifiers such as C4A copy number carry much of the risk. PMID:35729719 shows C4A dose matters in heterozygotes but the analogous analysis in complete C2 deficiency has not been done.

open_questions/1.rationale:
Narrowed from an earlier gap that asked the same question of vaccination and prophylaxis together and recorded that no treatments were curated. The vaccination half is now answered: PMID:22842196 studied vaccination in hereditary C2 deficiency itself, showing intact antibody titres and restored opsonophagocytosis through antibody-dependent alternative-pathway activation, which is C2-specific rather than class-level evidence.
The prophylaxis half is genuinely still open, and the two sources that bear on it point opposite ways without either settling it. The favourable one is two brothers followed for 21 years with no comparator arm and with vaccination given alongside, so it cannot isolate the antibiotic's contribution. The unfavourable one, a 77-patient European registry, found no association between prophylactic antibiotic use and subsequent infection risk — but it pooled mixed complement defects, of which C2 was 29%, so it cannot isolate C2 either. Both are curated on the treatment, the second as a REFUTE item.
What would close this is a C2-specific cohort with a prophylaxis comparator. Until then the treatment is curated as recommended practice with its evidence base shown as contested, rather than as an intervention of established benefit.

evidence.snippet: The Cri du Chat syndrome (CdCS) is a genetic disease resulting from a deletion of variable size occurring on the short arm of chromosome 5
evidence.explanation: States the causal lesion and its variable size.

evidence.snippet: results from the loss of genetic material at the distal region of the short arm of chromosome 5
evidence.explanation: Independent cohort confirmation of the causal lesion and its distal localisation.

steps/2.description: A heterozygous deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, ranging from well under 1 Mb to essentially the whole short arm. Terminal deletions predominate; interstitial deletions, unbalanced translocation products, ring chromosome 5 and mosaicism account for the remainder. This is a copy-number loss, not a point variant, so the pathogenic unit is an interval rather than a gene.

evidence.snippet: partial aneusomy syndromes like CdCS result from abnormal gene dosage (haploinsufficiency)
evidence.explanation: States the core dosage mechanism. The source continues "involving a large number of contiguous genes", but that phrase is hyphenated across a line break in the cached PDF text, so the quote stops at the preceding word.

evidence.snippet: MR increased as deletions that included MRI extended progressively into MRII and MRIII, and MR became profound when all three regions were deleted.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that cognitive severity is dose-additive across three separable intervals, which is the basis for the deletion-extent claim in this node.

steps/3.description: Reduced dosage of a large number of contiguous genes across the deleted interval. Because separable sub-intervals map to separable phenotypic components, this node fans out to region-specific consequences rather than acting as a single undifferentiated insult. Cognitive severity in particular scales with how much of the 5p interval is lost: three distinct regions contribute additively, so severity increases as the deletion extends across them.

evidence.snippet: the critical region for the cat-like cry is mapped to a short 640 kbp region on chromosome 5p
evidence.explanation: Fine-maps the cry determinant using patients who differ in the presence of the cry.

evidence.snippet: high-pitched cry seemed to map at p14.3–p13.2 bands versus bands p15.33–p15.31
evidence.explanation: Recorded as REFUTE because it directly contradicts the distal localisation this node asserts. The largest contemporary cohort mapped the cry to a much more proximal interval than every earlier study. The distal mapping is retained as the node's primary claim because it rests on phenotype dissection in patients who differ in the presence of the cry, which is the stronger design, but the disagreement is real and is flagged rather than suppressed.

steps/4.description: Reduced dosage of the small distal interval whose loss determines the cat-like cry. Phenotype-dissection studies comparing patients with and without the cry narrowed this interval to roughly 640 kb, and array-based mapping placed the cry determinant in 1.5 Mb of distal 5p15.31. The responsible gene or genes are not established; several candidates lie in the interval but none is proven.

evidence.snippet: Delta-catenin is an adherens junction protein involved in cell motility and expressed early in neuronal development.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the molecular identity and neurodevelopmental role of the gene product whose dosage is reduced.

steps/5.description: Reduced dosage of delta-catenin, a neuronal adherens-junction protein expressed early in neuronal development and involved in cell motility. This is the best-supported single-gene contributor in the syndrome: hemizygous loss correlates with cognitive severity in patients, and restoring the gene product rescues cognition in an engineered rodent model of the syntenic deletion.

evidence.snippet: Due to its role in guiding axons or migrating neuronal precursors during cortical development in mice
evidence.explanation: States the gene function on which the candidacy rests. The source continues that the SEMAF deletion "may be responsible for some of the features of CdCS"; that continuation is hyphenated across a line break in the cached PDF text and so cannot be quoted verbatim. The attribution is suggestive and rests on mouse data, hence PARTIAL.

steps/6.description: Reduced dosage of semaphorin 5A, an axon-guidance molecule implicated in guiding axons and migrating neuronal precursors during cortical development. A candidate contributor rather than an established driver.

evidence.snippet: limiting component for the telomerase activity that is essential for telomere-length maintenance and sustained cell proliferation
evidence.explanation: Establishes the molecular function lost. The full sentence begins "hTERT is the rate-limiting component..."; "rate-limiting" is split across a line break in the cached PDF text, so the quote starts after it. The clinical consequence in this syndrome remains proposed, hence PARTIAL.

steps/7.description: Reduced dosage of telomerase reverse transcriptase, the rate-limiting component of telomerase, which is required for telomere-length maintenance and sustained cell proliferation. Whether this contributes materially to the clinical phenotype is unresolved, and no downstream consequence is asserted here.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, this relative enrichment is not driven by changes in the methylation of genes on chromosome 5.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the methylation signal is independent of the deleted interval, which is what makes it a candidate modifier rather than a downstream readout of gene dosage.

evidence.snippet: revealed enrichment of genes controlling embryonic development and genes linked to symptoms which are among the most common symptoms of Cri du chat syndrome: developmental delay and microcephaly
evidence.explanation: Ties the methylation changes specifically to the developmental-delay and microcephaly phenotypes.

steps/8.description: Genome-wide DNA methylation differences in patients relative to matched controls, including at promoters of genes controlling embryonic development and at CpG sites linked to developmental delay and microcephaly. Critically, this enrichment is not driven by methylation changes on chromosome 5, so it is a candidate modifier layer acting outside the deleted interval that may help explain why patients with similar deletions differ clinically. Direction of causality is not established: the changes could contribute to phenotype or reflect it.

evidence.snippet: This model exhibits pronounced deficits in social behavior, cognition, and anxiety, accompanied by neuronal abnormalities and immune dysregulation in key brain regions such as the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC).
evidence.explanation: Documents the cellular and regional abnormalities in the engineered model.

steps/9.description: Reduced dendritic-arbor complexity and a shift away from mature mushroom-shaped dendritic spines in cortical and hippocampal neurons, with increased neuronal density in superficial layers. Demonstrated in the rat model of the syntenic deletion; the corresponding human neuropathology has not been characterised.

evidence.snippet: corpus callosum anomalies, and anomalies of cortical development
evidence.explanation: Documents abnormalities of cortical development among the neuroradiological findings in patients.

steps/10.description: Perturbed migration of neuronal precursors and abnormal cortical wiring, inferred from the developmental roles of the co-deleted guidance and adhesion molecules. Anomalies of cortical development are among the structural findings reported on patient neuroimaging.

evidence.snippet: of the larynx (small, narrow, diamond-shaped) and of the epiglottis (flabby, small, hypotonic)
evidence.explanation: Describes the laryngeal and epiglottic anatomy underlying the cry.

steps/11.description: A small, narrow, diamond-shaped larynx with a flabby, small, hypotonic epiglottis. This is the structural substrate of the cat-like cry and is also the reason intubation can be difficult in these patients, which makes it a mechanism node with direct perioperative relevance.

evidence.snippet: MRI analyses showed that isolated pontine hypoplasia is the most common finding, followed by vermian hypoplasia, ventricular anomalies
evidence.explanation: Establishes the pattern and relative frequency of hindbrain findings.

evidence.snippet: of the cranial base suggest associated anomalies of the brain (rhombencephalic region) and larynx during embryonal development
evidence.explanation: States the developmental hypothesis linking hindbrain and laryngeal maldevelopment. The sentence opens "Malformations of the cranial base..."; the first word is hyphenated across a line break in the cached PDF text, so the quote starts at the following word. Marked PARTIAL because the source frames it as a suggestion.

steps/12.description: Hypoplasia of hindbrain structures, most consistently the pons and cerebellar vermis on neuroimaging. This node carries the central component of the cry: cranial-base malformation has long been argued to imply concurrent maldevelopment of the rhombencephalic region and the larynx during embryogenesis, and pontine hypoplasia is the imaging correlate of that hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: MR depended approximately on the 5p deletion size and location, but there were many cases in which the retardation was disproportionately severe, given the 5p deletion. All 15 of these cases, approximately two-thirds of the severely retarded patients, were found to have copy-number aberrations in addition to the 5p deletion.
evidence.explanation: Supports both the deletion-size dependence and the second-lesion caveat that qualifies it.

steps/13.description: Reduced brain growth and impaired cortical function, manifesting as microcephaly with severe psychomotor and intellectual disability. Severity tracks deletion extent, but with an important caveat: a substantial share of the most severely affected patients carry additional copy-number changes outside 5p, so unusually severe impairment should prompt a search for a second lesion rather than being attributed to 5p deletion size alone.

evidence.snippet: partial aneusomy syndromes like CdCS result from abnormal gene dosage
evidence.explanation: States that the deletion acts through abnormal gene dosage.

edges/2.description: Loss of one copy of the interval reduces dosage of every gene it contains.

evidence.snippet: Genotype-phenotype correlations localized the region associated with the cry to 1.5 Mb in distal 5p15.31
evidence.explanation: Localises the cry determinant to a specific sub-interval of the deletion.

edges/3.description: Deletions extending into the distal cry interval remove its dosage-sensitive content; deletions sparing it generally spare the cry.

evidence.snippet: The genomic structure of the human delta-catenin gene (Human Gene Nomenclature Committee-approved symbol CTNND2) was determined and mapped to 5p15.2.
evidence.explanation: Places CTNND2 inside the deleted interval.

edges/4.description: CTNND2 lies at 5p15.2 and is removed by essentially all deletions large enough to produce the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: covering at least 10% of this region has been cloned
evidence.explanation: The sentence this clause completes is "The human Semaphorin F gene (SEMAF) covering at least 10% of this region has been cloned", placing SEMA5A/SEMAF inside the 5p15.2 critical region. The quote starts mid-sentence because "Semaphorin" is hyphenated across a line break in the cached PDF text.

edges/5.description: SEMA5A maps to the 5p15 critical region and is co-deleted.

evidence.snippet: haploinsufficiency of the telomerase reverse transcriptase (hTERT) gene, localised to 5p15.33
evidence.explanation: Places TERT inside the deleted interval and frames its loss as haploinsufficiency.

edges/6.description: TERT lies at 5p15.33 and is removed by terminal deletions.

evidence.snippet: MRI analyses showed that isolated pontine hypoplasia is the most common finding, followed by vermian hypoplasia
evidence.explanation: Establishes hindbrain hypoplasia as a consistent structural consequence in patients with 5p deletions.

edges/7.description: Deletion of 5p is associated with structural hindbrain anomalies, of which pontine hypoplasia is the most frequent on neuroimaging. The intermediate genes and developmental steps are not established.

evidence.snippet: The characteristic cat-like cry is probably due to anomalies
evidence.explanation: The source attributes the cry to laryngeal and epiglottic anomalies but hedges the attribution ("probably"), so the edge is marked PARTIAL.

edges/8.description: Loss of the interval is associated with maldevelopment of the larynx and epiglottis. The molecular route from dosage loss to laryngeal structure is not established.

evidence.snippet: it is demonstrated that early gene replacement therapy with AAV-Ctnnd2 alleviates cognitive impairments in CdCS rats
evidence.explanation: Interventional rescue in an engineered model of the syntenic deletion, establishing that reduced Ctnnd2 dosage is causal for the cognitive phenotype in that model. Rodent evidence, so it supports the mechanism rather than the human phenotype directly.

evidence.snippet: However, the effectiveness of this therapy is confined to the early developmental stages and does not fully restore all CdCS symptoms.
evidence.explanation: The same source's own statement of the rescue's limits. Marked PARTIAL because it qualifies rather than supports the causal edge: single-gene restoration helps within a developmental window but does not correct the phenotype, which is consistent with the multi-gene dosage model this entry argues for.

edges/9.description: Reduced delta-catenin dosage impairs dendritic arbor complexity and the maturation of dendritic spines. Causality is supported by rescue: AAV-mediated Ctnnd2 replacement alleviates the cognitive phenotype in the rat model, which is an interventional test rather than a correlation. The source states the limits directly: the benefit is confined to early developmental stages and does not fully restore the phenotype, so this edge should not be read as establishing that restoring one co-deleted gene corrects the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: are potentially involved in cerebral development and their deletion may be associated with mental retardation in CdCS patients
evidence.explanation: Supports the proposed developmental route while making its provisional status explicit.

edges/10.description: Loss of one copy of an axon-guidance molecule is proposed to perturb neuronal migration and cortical wiring. The step is inferred from gene function rather than demonstrated in patients.

evidence.snippet: This model exhibits pronounced deficits in social behavior, cognition, and anxiety
evidence.explanation: Links the cellular deficits to organism-level cognitive impairment in the model.

edges/11.description: Synaptic and dendritic deficits converge on impaired cortical function.

evidence.snippet: are potentially involved in cerebral development and their deletion may be associated with mental retardation in CdCS patients
evidence.explanation: Supports the proposed link from disrupted cerebral development to the cognitive phenotype, with the source's provisional framing preserved.

edges/12.description: Disordered migration and wiring impair forebrain growth and function.

evidence.snippet: is suggestive of epigenetic changes early in embryonic development that may be contributing to the development of symptoms
evidence.explanation: The authors' own framing of the possible contribution, stated as suggestive rather than demonstrated, which is why this is PARTIAL.

evidence.snippet: with the present data we cannot conclude about the sequence of events between DNA methylation changes and other cellular functions
evidence.explanation: The source explicitly disclaims knowledge of causal ordering. Recorded here so the UNKNOWN edge typing is justified from the literature rather than being a curator hedge.

edges/13.description: The methylation changes may contribute to the neurodevelopmental phenotype, but the direction of the relationship is explicitly unresolved by the source study: the differences could be driving the phenotype, result from other epigenetic changes, or merely reflect altered gene expression. The edge is therefore typed UNKNOWN rather than asserted as causal, and it is retained because the modifier hypothesis is the leading explanation on offer for why patients with comparable deletions differ clinically.

evidence.snippet: A strong correlation was found between the hemizygous loss of delta-catenin and severe mental retardation.
evidence.explanation: Directly links CTNND2 hemizygosity to cognitive severity in patients with 5p terminal deletions.

genes/0.notes: Delta-catenin, a neuronal adherens-junction protein at 5p15.2 involved in cell motility and expressed early in neuronal development. Hemizygous loss correlates with severe intellectual disability in patients, and AAV-mediated Ctnnd2 replacement rescues cognitive deficits in a rat model of the syntenic deletion. Typed COOPERATING rather than CAUSATIVE because it is one of several co-deleted contributors, not sufficient on its own for the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Two genes, Semaphorin F (SEMAF) and delta-catenin (CTNND2), which have been mapped to the "critical regions", are potentially involved in cerebral development and their deletion may be associated with mental retardation in CdCS patients.
evidence.explanation: Names SEMA5A/SEMAF as a critical-region gene implicated in the cognitive phenotype. The hedged wording ("potentially", "may be") supports a candidate role only, so this is marked PARTIAL.

genes/1.notes: Semaphorin 5A (historically SEMAF), an axon-guidance molecule mapping to the 5p15 critical region and implicated in guiding axons and migrating neuronal precursors during cortical development. Candidate-gene status: the source attribution is explicitly probabilistic.

evidence.snippet: Deletion of the telomerase reverse transcriptase (hTERT) gene, localised to 5p15.33, could contribute to the phenotypic changes in CdCS.
evidence.explanation: Supports TERT as a candidate contributor only; the source states this as a possibility ("could contribute"), so the evidence is marked PARTIAL.

genes/2.notes: Telomerase reverse transcriptase at 5p15.33, the rate-limiting component of telomerase. Included in the deletion in most patients, but its contribution to the clinical phenotype remains proposed rather than established, hence the UNKNOWN typing.

evidence.snippet: A de novo deletion is present in 85% of the patients. Ten to 15% are familial cases with more than 90% due to a parental translocation and 5% due to an inversion of chromosome 5.
evidence.explanation: Gives the de novo vs familial breakdown and the mechanisms of familial cases.

evidence.snippet: The origin of the deleted chromosome 5 was paternal in 55 out of 61 patients (90.2%).
evidence.explanation: Documents the predominantly paternal origin of the deleted chromosome.

genes/3.notes: Partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (copy-number loss), of variable size; severity correlates with deletion size. About 85% are de novo; 10-15% are familial, most often from a parental balanced translocation (and ~5% a parental inversion). The deleted chromosome is of paternal origin in ~90% of de novo cases. No coordinate slot exists in the schema; the structural event is recorded here in prose (copy-number loss, 5p15).

evidence.snippet: There is no specific therapy for CdCS but early rehabilitative and educational interventions improve the prognosis and considerable progress has been made in the social adjustment of CdCS patients.
evidence.explanation: States both the absence of specific therapy and the benefit of early intervention.

treatments/0.description: No disease-specific therapy exists. Early rehabilitative and educational intervention is the mainstay and measurably improves prognosis and social adjustment, which makes prompt diagnosis worthwhile even though the underlying lesion is not correctable.

evidence.snippet: Early rehabilitation (physical therapy, psychomotricity, speech therapy) is recommended for the neurological problems
evidence.explanation: Names speech therapy explicitly among the recommended early rehabilitative modalities.

treatments/1.description: Speech therapy alongside physical therapy and psychomotricity. Expressive language is impaired out of proportion to comprehension, which is the specific rationale for prioritising expressive-language and augmentative communication work rather than general developmental support.

evidence.snippet: The risk of recurrence is practically negligible for the cases of a de novo deletion, which are the most frequent.
evidence.explanation: The counselling figure for the majority mechanism. Paired with the translocation-carrier risk recorded under inheritance, this is what the counselling session actually conveys.

treatments/2.description: Counselling turns on which mechanism produced the deletion. A de novo deletion carries negligible recurrence risk; a parental balanced translocation carries a risk of unbalanced offspring roughly an order of magnitude higher, and makes prenatal diagnosis appropriate. Parental karyotyping after a new diagnosis is what separates the two, and residual gonadal mosaicism qualifies even the negligible figure.

treatments/3.description: For hypotonia and psychomotor delay.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that one candidate gene, FLJ25076, encodes a ubiquitin-conjugated enzyme E2 type, which is locally expressed in thoracic and scalp tissues.
evidence.explanation: Documents the state of the art on the cry interval: the leading candidate is offered only as a suggestion, with tissue expression that does not obviously implicate the larynx. This is the evidence that the gap remains open.

open_questions/0.rationale: The cry is the syndrome's defining feature and its determining interval has been narrowed to roughly 640 kb by phenotype dissection, yet no responsible gene has been established. The interval is gene-rich, and the candidates characterised so far are either ubiquitously expressed or have no known role in laryngeal development, so none offers a satisfying mechanistic account. This leaves the best-mapped genotype-phenotype relationship in the syndrome without a molecular explanation.

evidence.snippet: The immunostaining and RNA-seq analyses provide new insights into CdCS pathogenesis, revealing inflammatory and immune processes.
evidence.explanation: Source of the inflammatory and immune findings whose human validity is the subject of this mismatch. Rodent evidence, which is precisely why the human counterpart is an open question rather than settled mechanism.

open_questions/1.rationale: The engineered rat model reproduces cognitive and social deficits and shows immune dysregulation in hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, and AAV-Ctnnd2 rescue makes the CTNND2 dosage link causal in that system. But the immune and synaptic-pruning arm has no human counterpart evidence: no patient neuropathology series has looked for astrocyte reactivity or complement activation. The gap matters therapeutically, because a neuroinflammatory component would suggest targets entirely different from gene replacement, and it would be easy to over-read the rodent result as established human mechanism.

evidence.snippet: with the present data we cannot conclude about the sequence of events between DNA methylation changes and other cellular functions
evidence.explanation: The authors state the causal-direction gap themselves, so this discussion records an acknowledged limitation of the primary study rather than a curator-invented doubt.

open_questions/2.rationale: Methylation changes enriched at developmental-delay and microcephaly genes, demonstrably not driven by chromosome 5, are an attractive explanation for why patients with similar deletions differ clinically. But the study design is cross-sectional and measured in blood, so it cannot distinguish a modifier that shapes the phenotype from a signature that reflects it. Resolving the direction determines whether this is a therapeutic target or merely a biomarker.

evidence.snippet: mapped in chromosome 5 short arm, are known to be expressed in the brain, and to play a role in the development of the nervous system
evidence.explanation: Groups TERT with SEMA5A and CTNND2 as brain-expressed 5p genes whose haploinsufficiency is proposed but not resolved, which is precisely the open question.

evidence.snippet: the mechanism of which has remained unexplained
evidence.explanation: States that the mechanism linking 5p gene dosage to developmental impairment is unexplained, supporting the gap rather than any particular resolution.

open_questions/3.rationale: TERT sits at 5p15.33 and is removed by essentially every terminal deletion, so it is routinely listed among the syndrome's candidate genes. But unlike CTNND2 it has no correlative human evidence and no rescue experiment, and no telomere phenotype has been demonstrated in patients. This node is deliberately left without a downstream edge for that reason: asserting one would manufacture a mechanism the literature does not support. The question matters because proximity to the telomere makes TERT loss near-universal, so if it were contributing it would be contributing in almost every patient.

evidence.snippet: We have identified a missense point mutation in the gene coding for beta -actin that results in an arginine-to-tryptophan substitution at position 183.
evidence.explanation: The identification of the variant in the original family.

evidence.snippet: The two dominant heterozygous gain-of-function β-actin mutations p.R183W and p.E364K were identified in patients with developmental malformations, deafness and juvenile-onset dystonia (p.R183W) and neutrophil dysfunction (p.E364K).
evidence.explanation: The source of the GAIN_OF_FUNCTION category recorded here. The authors class it that way on biochemical grounds; note the functional consequence is altered dynamics rather than increased activity in any simple sense, which is why the next node states the mechanism rather than leaving the label to carry it.

steps/1.description: A recurrent heterozygous missense change at a residue adjacent to the nucleotide-binding pocket of cytoplasmic beta-actin. It is the same variant in essentially every reported patient, which is unusual enough to be worth stating: this is not an allelic series, it is one substitution.

evidence.snippet: establishes an unusual stacking interaction with Tyr69 that perturbs nucleotide release from actin monomers and polymerization behavior by inducing a closed state conformation.
evidence.explanation: The structural mechanism, from recombinant protein assays and molecular dynamics.

steps/2.description:
The tryptophan stacks against Tyr69. That interaction perturbs nucleotide release from the monomer and biases it towards a closed conformation, which is what changes its polymerization behaviour. Recombinant protein work and molecular dynamics simulation agree on the mechanism.
The modifier is ABNORMAL rather than DECREASED, and the reason is about export rather than about the biology. A closed nucleotide cleft retains its nucleotide, so what falls is exchange, not binding - but the bound term is GO:0000166 nucleotide binding, and kgx_export drops preferred_term and emits only the term id plus a direction qualifier. DECREASED here would put "beta-actin nucleotide binding is decreased" into the knowledge graph, which is the inverse of what the source reports. GO has no term for the exchange step itself, so the honest pairing is the binding term with a non-directional modifier.

evidence.snippet: Cellular studies of a lymphoblastoid cell line obtained from an affected patient demonstrated morphological abnormalities of the actin cytoskeleton and altered actin depolymerization dynamics in response to latrunculin A, an actin monomer-sequestering drug.
evidence.explanation: The cellular phenotype in patient-derived cells.

evidence.snippet: Resistance to latrunculin A was also observed in NIH 3T3 cells expressing the mutant actin.
evidence.explanation: Reproduction in a heterologous cell line, which is what makes this a property of the mutant protein rather than of the patient background.

steps/3.description: The cellular readout, and the finding the disease was named from. Patient lymphoblastoid cells show a morphologically abnormal actin cytoskeleton and altered depolymerization kinetics when challenged with latrunculin A, a monomer-sequestering drug; the resistance is reproduced in fibroblasts expressing the mutant actin, so it is a property of the protein rather than of the patient's cells. The modifiers are DYSREGULATED and ABNORMAL rather than DECREASED because that is as far as the source goes: it reports "altered" depolymerization dynamics and "morphological abnormalities" of the cytoskeleton. Latrunculin resistance does suggest disassembly is harder to induce, but that reading is an inference, and the node is named for the alteration rather than for a direction.

evidence.snippet: We found that, although cytoplasmic actin is necessary, neither β-actin nor γ-actin is required for normal stereocilia development or auditory function in young animals.
evidence.explanation: The negative half: development does not need this isoform specifically.

evidence.snippet: However, aging mice with β-actin- or γ-actin-deficient hair cells develop different patterns of progressive hearing loss and distinct pathogenic changes in stereocilia morphology, despite colocalization of the actin isoforms.
evidence.explanation: The positive half: maintenance does. Note this is a deletion model and the human lesion is a missense change with altered dynamics, so the model supports the compartment and the developmental timing rather than the molecular mechanism.

steps/4.description: The stereociliary core is an actin bundle. The mouse experiment that makes this branch credible is a negative one as much as a positive one: conditional deletion of Actb in hair cells leaves stereocilia development and young-animal hearing intact, and only produces progressive hearing loss with age. A maintenance defect rather than a developmental one is exactly what infant-onset progressive deafness from a constitutive variant needs.

evidence.snippet: In this patient with dystonia-deafness syndrome caused by ACTB p.Arg183Trp heterozygosity, unprecedented brain imaging findings strongly indicate striatal neuronal/dopaminergic dysfunction as the underlying cause of the dystonia.
evidence.explanation: Locates the lesion in the striatum in a living patient. It does not establish that the cellular cause is actin turnover, which is the inferred part of this node - hence directness INDIRECT, which puts that caveat in a slot rather than only in this sentence.

steps/5.description: Dendritic spines are actin structures and their turnover is continuous, so a subtly abnormal actin is a chronic burden on striatal projection neurons rather than an acute one. That is the proposed reason the dystonia waits for adolescence.

evidence.snippet: We hypothesize that the pleiotropic manifestations of the dystonia-deafness syndrome caused by this mutation derive from diverse developmental functions of beta-actin in neural crest migration and proliferation (facial dysmorphogenesis), hair cell stereocilia function (infant-onset deafness), and altered synaptic activity patterns associated with pubertal changes in striatal function (adolescent-onset dystonia).
evidence.explanation: The proposal itself, quoted with its own hedge intact. Graded INDIRECT because the sentence is a hypothesis about what beta-actin does in the neural crest, not a measurement of migration in this variant - the node description already says no migration assay has been reported.

steps/6.description: Actin-driven lamellipodial motility carries neural crest cells to the face. This is the weakest of the three branches - it is a mechanism proposed to explain the craniofacial findings, with no migration assay reported for this variant - and it is recorded at that strength.

evidence.snippet: Both Epidepride-SPECT and FDG-PET showed reduced tracer uptake in the striatum bilaterally, particularly in the putamen.
evidence.explanation: The two imaging modalities and the anatomical distribution. This is the strongest in vivo human evidence in the entry.

steps/7.description: Measured, not inferred. Epidepride-SPECT shows reduced D2-receptor binding and FDG-PET reduced glucose uptake, both bilaterally and worst in the putamen, while the presynaptic dopamine-transporter scan is only slightly abnormal. The pattern is a postsynaptic and metabolic striatal deficit rather than nigrostriatal denervation, which is why this entry does not conform the node to the parkinsonism module.

evidence.snippet: ACTB p.Arg183Trp heterozygosity has been reported in six patients to cause combined infant-onset deafness and dystonia manifesting in adolescence or young adulthood.
evidence.explanation: Both the phenotype and its timing, across the reported series rather than a single case.

evidence.snippet: Our patient has severe, intractable dystonia, developmental delay, and sensorineural hearing loss, besides hyperintensities in the caudate nuclei and putamen on the brain MRI, which is a distinct but overlapping phenotype with the previously reported case of identical twins with the same alteration in ACTB.
evidence.explanation: Severity, and the basal-ganglia MRI signal change that accompanies it. Also the sentence that records this case as lacking midline malformation, which is the basis for the incomplete-penetrance note below.

steps/8.description: Onset in adolescence or young adulthood, progressive, and often severe enough to be life-threatening. Bulbar involvement with velopharyngeal insufficiency and dysphagia is reported.

evidence.snippet: ACTB p.Arg183Trp heterozygosity has been reported in six patients to cause combined infant-onset deafness and dystonia manifesting in adolescence or young adulthood.
evidence.explanation: Records the deafness and its infant onset across the reported patients.

steps/9.description: Infant-onset, and typically the first manifestation. Cochlear implantation is the usual management.

evidence.snippet: The disease phenotype includes developmental midline malformations, sensory hearing loss, and a delayed-onset generalized dystonia syndrome in monozygotic twins.
evidence.explanation: The malformations as originally described.

evidence.snippet: The previously reported twins with same p.Arg183Trp mutation as our patient had midline facial defects and skeletal anomalies; however our patient did not display these features of the phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Graded REFUTE against the claim that this phenotype is constant, not against the disease: the same variant in this patient produced none of the midline features the twins had. An earlier revision quoted the case-identity sentence instead and justified it by saying the abstract does not restate the negative finding. That was wrong - this cache is full_text_xml, and the sentence above is in it verbatim. The claim about what the source contains was never checked against the source.

steps/10.description: Mild dysmorphic features, and the least consistent of the three phenotypes. The original twins had developmental midline malformations; a later patient with the identical variant was explicitly non-dysmorphic.

evidence.snippet: Arg183 is located near the nucleotide-binding pocket of actin.
evidence.explanation: Places the substituted residue where it can act on nucleotide handling, which is the structural basis of this edge.

evidence.snippet: We hypothesize that the pleiotropic manifestations of the dystonia-deafness syndrome caused by this mutation derive from diverse developmental functions of beta-actin in neural crest migration and proliferation (facial dysmorphogenesis), hair cell stereocilia function (infant-onset deafness), and altered synaptic activity patterns associated with pubertal changes in striatal function (adolescent-onset dystonia).
evidence.explanation: The temporal-vulnerability model that all three branch edges rest on. The authors present it as a hypothesis and this entry marks the edges indirect for that reason.

edges/3.description: Inferred for this variant. The step is supported by mouse Actb deletion in hair cells, not by any experiment on p.Arg183Trp cochlea.

evidence.snippet: We hypothesize that the pleiotropic manifestations of the dystonia-deafness syndrome caused by this mutation derive from diverse developmental functions of beta-actin in neural crest migration and proliferation (facial dysmorphogenesis), hair cell stereocilia function (infant-onset deafness), and altered synaptic activity patterns associated with pubertal changes in striatal function (adolescent-onset dystonia).
evidence.explanation: Same hypothesis, the striatal branch.

evidence.snippet: We hypothesize that the pleiotropic manifestations of the dystonia-deafness syndrome caused by this mutation derive from diverse developmental functions of beta-actin in neural crest migration and proliferation (facial dysmorphogenesis), hair cell stereocilia function (infant-onset deafness), and altered synaptic activity patterns associated with pubertal changes in striatal function (adolescent-onset dystonia).
evidence.explanation: Same hypothesis, the craniofacial branch.

evidence.snippet: We have identified a missense point mutation in the gene coding for beta -actin that results in an arginine-to-tryptophan substitution at position 183.
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease assignment and the variant.

evidence.snippet: The two dominant heterozygous gain-of-function β-actin mutations p.R183W and p.E364K were identified in patients with developmental malformations, deafness and juvenile-onset dystonia (p.R183W) and neutrophil dysfunction (p.E364K).
evidence.explanation: Supports the variant-specific framing in the notes: two ACTB variants, two unrelated phenotypes, studied side by side.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous c.547C>T, p.Arg183Trp, in essentially every reported patient. ACTB is highly pleiotropic: other variants cause Baraitser-Winter cerebrofrontofacial syndrome type 1 (curated separately), and p.Glu364Lys causes a neutrophil dysfunction phenotype. The three are separated by variant and by mechanism rather than by gene, which is why this record is variant-specific and says so.

evidence.snippet: Pallidal stimulation provided a substantial improvement of the severe generalized dystonia, which is largely sustained at 4-year follow-up, and we advise this treatment to be considered in such patients.
evidence.explanation: The outcome and the authors' recommendation, with the four-year durability that makes it more than a short-term response.

evidence.snippet: Our study expands and confirms the complex phenotypic spectrum of ACTB gene-related disorders and supports the effectiveness of pallidal stimulation on motor outcomes and quality of life in dystonia due to ACTB p.Arg183Trp heterozygosity.
evidence.explanation: An independent patient with long-term benefit, which is what takes this from one case to a reproduced observation.

treatments/0.description: Stimulation of the postero-ventral internal pallidum. This is the only intervention in the entry with a measured outcome in this disease, and the effect is large and sustained: the Burke-Fahn-Marsden motor score fell from 87 preoperatively to 21 at 2.5 months and was still 30 at four years. A second reported patient also benefited long-term.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Modulates basal-ganglia output downstream of the striatal deficit; it does not address the actin lesion.

evidence.snippet: Significant improvement of motor function (Burke‐Fahn‐Marsden's Dystonia Rating Scales–Dystonia Movement Scale ... 44 vs. 20) was observed at the 12‐month follow‐up
evidence.explanation: The quantified outcome: the Burke-Fahn-Marsden motor score halved at one year. The ellipsis elides the source's own bracketed abbreviation of the scale name, "[BFMDRS-M]", and nothing else. It is elided rather than quoted because the reference validator strips bracketed spans from the query side only, keeping them literal just for spans matching "^[A-Z]{2,}$" - which a hyphenated abbreviation cannot match. Quoted otherwise with the source's own typography, which uses Unicode hyphens throughout.

evidence.snippet: The greatest BFMDRS‐M improvements were observed for the arm (66.7%) and leg (53.8%) dystonia, with less clinical impact on the neck and trunk.
evidence.explanation: The distribution of the benefit, recorded because a single summary score hides it. Arm and leg dystonia improved by roughly two thirds and one half; neck and trunk did not follow.

treatments/1.description: A second, different stimulation target with its own measured outcome.
